LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory

Five hundred questions, each with its own haystack of chat sessions about 115k tokens long. One or more sessions hold the evidence, and retrieval is scored as recall of those sessions against the benchmark’s own

. Every session is embedded turn by turn and ranked by its best turn — 4,846 sessions and 199,641 turns. ALL@5 is the share of questions whose every evidence session is in the top five; ANY@5 is the share with at least one.
vectors. The cosine column ranks a session by its best turn’s cosine. The engine column ranks it by its best turn under the engine’s score, with the configuration frozen on LoCoMo dev at
— nothing was tuned on this benchmark, so all 500 questions are the report.

Every evidence session is in the top five for 90.6% of questions against 85.8% for cosine, and in the top ten for 97.0% against 93.4%. The largest gains are multi-session, where ALL@5 moves from 75.9 to 85.7, and temporal-reasoning, from 75.9 to 81.2. LongMemEval has no fact layer, so the engine’s fact, entity and typed-graph generators propose nothing here; what does the work is lexical match, the session timeline, adjacency and a second hop.

Session recall is not answer accuracy. Systems reporting LongMemEval scores in the high eighties usually report an end-to-end answer metric with a language-model judge, which is a different measurement and not comparable to these columns. The run uses the release the dataset card now marks deprecated in favour of a cleaned one.
